5439// We don't want to require the users to write TypesN<...> directly,
5440// as that would require them to count the length. Types<...> is much
5441// easier to write, but generates horrible messages when there is a
5442// compiler error, as gcc insists on printing out each template
5443// argument, even if it has the default value (this means Types<int>
5444// will appear as Types<int, None, None, ..., None> in the compiler
5445// errors).
5446//
5447// Our solution is to combine the best part of the two approaches: a
5448// user would write Types<T1, ..., TN>, and Google Test will translate
5449// that to TypesN<T1, ..., TN> internally to make error messages
5450// readable. The translation is done by the 'type' member of the

6346# define GTEST_TEMPLATE_ template <typename T> class
6347
6348// The template "selector" struct TemplateSel<Tmpl> is used to
6349// represent Tmpl, which must be a class template with one type
6350// parameter, as a type. TemplateSel<Tmpl>::Bind<T>::type is defined
6351// as the type Tmpl<T>. This allows us to actually instantiate the
6352// template "selected" by TemplateSel<Tmpl>.
6353//
6354// This trick is necessary for simulating typedef for class templates,
6355// which C++ doesn't support directly.
6356template <GTEST_TEMPLATE_ Tmpl>
6357struct TemplateSel {
6358 template <typename T>
6359 struct Bind {
6360 typedef Tmpl<T> type;
6361 };
6362};
6363
6364# define GTEST_BIND_(TmplSel, T) \
6365 TmplSel::template Bind<T>::type
6366
6367// A unique struct template used as the default value for the
6368// arguments of class template Templates. This allows us to simulate
6369// variadic templates (e.g. Templates<int>, Templates<int, double>,
6370// and etc), which C++ doesn't support directly.
6371template <typename T>
6372struct NoneT {};
6373
6374// The following family of struct and struct templates are used to
6375// represent template lists. In particular, TemplatesN<T1, T2, ...,
6376// TN> represents a list of N templates (T1, T2, ..., and TN). Except
6377// for Templates0, every struct in the family has two member types:
6378// Head for the selector of the first template in the list, and Tail
6379// for the rest of the list.
6380
6381// The empty template list.
6382struct Templates0 {};
6383
6384// Template lists of length 1, 2, 3, and so on.
6385
6386template <GTEST_TEMPLATE_ T1>
6387struct Templates1 {
6388 typedef TemplateSel<T1> Head;
6389 typedef Templates0 Tail;
6390};
6391template <GTEST_TEMPLATE_ T1, GTEST_TEMPLATE_ T2>
6392struct Templates2 {
6393 typedef TemplateSel<T1> Head;
6394 typedef Templates1<T2> Tail;
6395};

6398struct Templates3 {
6399 typedef TemplateSel<T1> Head;
6400 typedef Templates2<T2, T3> Tail;
6401};

8057// Due to C++ preprocessor weirdness, we need double indirection to
8058// concatenate two tokens when one of them is __LINE__. Writing
8059//
8060// foo ## __LINE__
8061//
8062// will result in the token foo__LINE__, instead of foo followed by
8063// the current line number. For more details, see
8064// http://www.parashift.com/c++-faq-lite/misc-technical-issues.html#faq-39.6
8065#define GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(foo, bar) GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_IMPL_(foo, bar)
8066#define GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_IMPL_(foo, bar) foo ## bar

8098// Two overloaded helpers for checking at compile time whether an
8099// expression is a null pointer literal (i.e. NULL or any 0-valued
8100// compile-time integral constant). Their return values have
8101// different sizes, so we can use sizeof() to test which version is
8102// picked by the compiler. These helpers have no implementations, as
8103// we only need their signatures.
8104//
8105// Given IsNullLiteralHelper(x), the compiler will pick the first
8106// version if x can be implicitly converted to Secret*, and pick the
8107// second version otherwise. Since Secret is a secret and incomplete
8108// type, the only expression a user can write that has type Secret* is
8109// a null pointer literal. Therefore, we know that x is a null
8110// pointer literal if and only if the first version is picked by the
8111// compiler.
8112char IsNullLiteralHelper(Secret* p);
8113char (&IsNullLiteralHelper(...))[2]; // NOLINT
8114
8115// A compile-time bool constant that is true if and only if x is a
8116// null pointer literal (i.e. NULL or any 0-valued compile-time
8117// integral constant).
8118#ifdef GTEST_ELLIPSIS_NEEDS_POD_
8119// We lose support for NULL detection where the compiler doesn't like
8120// passing non-POD classes through ellipsis (...).
8121# define GTEST_IS_NULL_LITERAL_(x) false
8122#else
8123# define GTEST_IS_NULL_LITERAL_(x) \
8124 (sizeof(::testing::internal::IsNullLiteralHelper(x)) == 1)
8125#endif // GTEST_ELLIPSIS_NEEDS_POD_

8136// This exception is thrown by (and only by) a failed Google Test
8137// assertion when GTEST_FLAG(throw_on_failure) is true (if exceptions
8138// are enabled). We derive it from std::runtime_error, which is for
8139// errors presumably detectable only at run time. Since
8140// std::runtime_error inherits from std::exception, many testing
8141// frameworks know how to extract and print the message inside it.
8142class GTEST_API_ GoogleTestFailureException : public ::std::runtime_error {
8143 public:
8144 explicit GoogleTestFailureException(const TestPartResult& failure);
8145};

8147GTEST_DISABLE_MSC_WARNINGS_POP_() // 4275

8151namespace edit_distance {
8152// Returns the optimal edits to go from 'left' to 'right'.
8153// All edits cost the same, with replace having lower priority than
8154// add/remove.
8155// Simple implementation of the Wagner-Fischer algorithm.
8156// See http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagner-Fischer_algorithm
8157enum EditType { kMatch, kAdd, kRemove, kReplace };
8158GTEST_API_ std::vector<EditType> CalculateOptimalEdits(
8159 const std::vector<size_t>& left, const std::vector<size_t>& right);
8160
8161// Same as above, but the input is represented as strings.
8162GTEST_API_ std::vector<EditType> CalculateOptimalEdits(
8163 const std::vector<std::string>& left,
8164 const std::vector<std::string>& right);
8165
8166// Create a diff of the input strings in Unified diff format.
8167GTEST_API_ std::string CreateUnifiedDiff(const std::vector<std::string>& left,
8168 const std::vector<std::string>& right,
8169 size_t context = 2);
8170
8171} // namespace edit_distance

8173// Calculate the diff between 'left' and 'right' and return it in unified diff

8177GTEST_API_ std::string DiffStrings(const std::string& left,

8181// Constructs and returns the message for an equality assertion
8182// (e.g. ASSERT_EQ, EXPECT_STREQ, etc) failure.
8183//
8184// The first four parameters are the expressions used in the assertion
8185// and their values, as strings. For example, for ASSERT_EQ(foo, bar)
8186// where foo is 5 and bar is 6, we have:
8187//
8188// expected_expression: "foo"
8189// actual_expression: "bar"
8190// expected_value: "5"
8191// actual_value: "6"
8192//
8193// The ignoring_case parameter is true iff the assertion is a
8194// *_STRCASEEQ*. When it's true, the string " (ignoring case)" will
8195// be inserted into the message.
8196GTEST_API_ AssertionResult EqFailure(const char* expected_expression,
8197 const char* actual_expression,
8198 const std::string& expected_value,
8199 const std::string& actual_value,
8200 bool ignoring_case);

8202// Constructs a failure message for Boolean assertions such as EXPECT_TRUE.
8203GTEST_API_ std::string GetBoolAssertionFailureMessage(
8204 const AssertionResult& assertion_result,
8205 const char* expression_text,
8206 const char* actual_predicate_value,
8207 const char* expected_predicate_value);

8209// This template class represents an IEEE floating-point number
8210// (either single-precision or double-precision, depending on the
8211// template parameters).
8212//
8213// The purpose of this class is to do more sophisticated number
8214// comparison. (Due to round-off error, etc, it's very unlikely that
8215// two floating-points will be equal exactly. Hence a naive
8216// comparison by the == operation often doesn't work.)
8217//
8218// Format of IEEE floating-point:
8219//
8220// The most-significant bit being the leftmost, an IEEE
8221// floating-point looks like
8222//
8223// sign_bit exponent_bits fraction_bits
8224//
8225// Here, sign_bit is a single bit that designates the sign of the
8226// number.
8227//
8228// For float, there are 8 exponent bits and 23 fraction bits.
8229//
8230// For double, there are 11 exponent bits and 52 fraction bits.
8231//
8232// More details can be found at
8233// http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_floating-point_standard.
8234//
8235// Template parameter:
8236//
8237// RawType: the raw floating-point type (either float or double)
8238template <typename RawType>
8239class FloatingPoint {
8240 public:
8241 // Defines the unsigned integer type that has the same size as the
8242 // floating point number.
8243 typedef typename TypeWithSize<sizeof(RawType)>::UInt Bits;
8244
8245 // Constants.
8246
8247 // # of bits in a number.
8248 static const size_t kBitCount = 8*sizeof(RawType);
8249
8250 // # of fraction bits in a number.
8251 static const size_t kFractionBitCount =
8252 std::numeric_limits<RawType>::digits - 1;
8253
8254 // # of exponent bits in a number.
8255 static const size_t kExponentBitCount = kBitCount - 1 - kFractionBitCount;
8256
8257 // The mask for the sign bit.
8258 static const Bits kSignBitMask = static_cast<Bits>(1) << (kBitCount - 1);
8259
8260 // The mask for the fraction bits.
8261 static const Bits kFractionBitMask =
8262 ~static_cast<Bits>(0) >> (kExponentBitCount + 1);
8263
8264 // The mask for the exponent bits.
8265 static const Bits kExponentBitMask = ~(kSignBitMask | kFractionBitMask);
8266
8267 // How many ULP's (Units in the Last Place) we want to tolerate when
8268 // comparing two numbers. The larger the value, the more error we
8269 // allow. A 0 value means that two numbers must be exactly the same
8270 // to be considered equal.
8271 //
8272 // The maximum error of a single floating-point operation is 0.5
8273 // units in the last place. On Intel CPU's, all floating-point
8274 // calculations are done with 80-bit precision, while double has 64
8275 // bits. Therefore, 4 should be enough for ordinary use.
8276 //
8277 // See the following article for more details on ULP:
8278 // http://randomascii.wordpress.com/2012/02/25/comparing-floating-point-numbers-2012-edition/
8279 static const size_t kMaxUlps = 4;
8280
8281 // Constructs a FloatingPoint from a raw floating-point number.
8282 //
8283 // On an Intel CPU, passing a non-normalized NAN (Not a Number)
8284 // around may change its bits, although the new value is guaranteed
8285 // to be also a NAN. Therefore, don't expect this constructor to
8286 // preserve the bits in x when x is a NAN.
8287 explicit FloatingPoint(const RawType& x) { u_.value_ = x; }
8288
8289 // Static methods
8290
8291 // Reinterprets a bit pattern as a floating-point number.
8292 //
8293 // This function is needed to test the AlmostEquals() method.
8294 static RawType ReinterpretBits(const Bits bits) {
8295 FloatingPoint fp(0);
8296 fp.u_.bits_ = bits;
8297 return fp.u_.value_;
8298 }
8299
8300 // Returns the floating-point number that represent positive infinity.
8301 static RawType Infinity() {
8302 return ReinterpretBits(kExponentBitMask);
8303 }
8304
8305 // Returns the maximum representable finite floating-point number.
8306 static RawType Max();
8307
8308 // Non-static methods
8309
8310 // Returns the bits that represents this number.
8311 const Bits &bits() const { return u_.bits_; }
8312
8313 // Returns the exponent bits of this number.
8314 Bits exponent_bits() const { return kExponentBitMask & u_.bits_; }
8315
8316 // Returns the fraction bits of this number.
8317 Bits fraction_bits() const { return kFractionBitMask & u_.bits_; }
8318
8319 // Returns the sign bit of this number.
8320 Bits sign_bit() const { return kSignBitMask & u_.bits_; }
8321
8322 // Returns true iff this is NAN (not a number).
8323 bool is_nan() const {
8324 // It's a NAN if the exponent bits are all ones and the fraction
8325 // bits are not entirely zeros.
8326 return (exponent_bits() == kExponentBitMask) && (fraction_bits() != 0);
8327 }
8328
8329 // Returns true iff this number is at most kMaxUlps ULP's away from
8330 // rhs. In particular, this function:
8331 //
8332 // - returns false if either number is (or both are) NAN.
8333 // - treats really large numbers as almost equal to infinity.
8334 // - thinks +0.0 and -0.0 are 0 DLP's apart.
8335 bool AlmostEquals(const FloatingPoint& rhs) const {
8336 // The IEEE standard says that any comparison operation involving
8337 // a NAN must return false.
8338 if (is_nan() || rhs.is_nan()) return false;
8339
8340 return DistanceBetweenSignAndMagnitudeNumbers(u_.bits_, rhs.u_.bits_)
8341 <= kMaxUlps;
8342 }
8343
8344 private:
8345 // The data type used to store the actual floating-point number.
8346 union FloatingPointUnion {
8347 RawType value_; // The raw floating-point number.
8348 Bits bits_; // The bits that represent the number.
8349 };
8350
8351 // Converts an integer from the sign-and-magnitude representation to
8352 // the biased representation. More precisely, let N be 2 to the
8353 // power of (kBitCount - 1), an integer x is represented by the
8354 // unsigned number x + N.
8355 //
8356 // For instance,
8357 //
8358 // -N + 1 (the most negative number representable using
8359 // sign-and-magnitude) is represented by 1;
8360 // 0 is represented by N; and
8361 // N - 1 (the biggest number representable using
8362 // sign-and-magnitude) is represented by 2N - 1.
8363 //
8364 // Read http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signed_number_representations
8365 // for more details on signed number representations.
8366 static Bits SignAndMagnitudeToBiased(const Bits &sam) {
8367 if (kSignBitMask & sam) {
8368 // sam represents a negative number.
8369 return ~sam + 1;
8370 } else {
8371 // sam represents a positive number.
8372 return kSignBitMask | sam;
8373 }
8374 }
8375
8376 // Given two numbers in the sign-and-magnitude representation,
8377 // returns the distance between them as an unsigned number.
8378 static Bits DistanceBetweenSignAndMagnitudeNumbers(const Bits &sam1,
8379 const Bits &sam2) {
8380 const Bits biased1 = SignAndMagnitudeToBiased(sam1);
8381 const Bits biased2 = SignAndMagnitudeToBiased(sam2);
8382 return (biased1 >= biased2) ? (biased1 - biased2) : (biased2 - biased1);
8383 }
8384
8385 FloatingPointUnion u_;
8386};

8388// We cannot use std::numeric_limits<T>::max() as it clashes with the max()
8389// macro defined by <windows.h>.
8390template <>
8391inline float FloatingPoint<float>::Max() { return FLT_MAX; }
8392template <>
8393inline double FloatingPoint<double>::Max() { return DBL_MAX; }

8400// In order to catch the mistake of putting tests that use different
8401// test fixture classes in the same test case, we need to assign
8402// unique IDs to fixture classes and compare them. The TypeId type is
8403// used to hold such IDs. The user should treat TypeId as an opaque
8404// type: the only operation allowed on TypeId values is to compare
8405// them for equality using the == operator.
8406typedef const void* TypeId;
8407
8408template <typename T>
8409class TypeIdHelper {
8410 public:
8411 // dummy_ must not have a const type. Otherwise an overly eager
8412 // compiler (e.g. MSVC 7.1 & 8.0) may try to merge
8413 // TypeIdHelper<T>::dummy_ for different Ts as an "optimization".
8414 static bool dummy_;
8415};
8416
8417template <typename T>
8418bool TypeIdHelper<T>::dummy_ = false;
8419
8420// GetTypeId<T>() returns the ID of type T. Different values will be
8421// returned for different types. Calling the function twice with the
8422// same type argument is guaranteed to return the same ID.
8423template <typename T>
8424TypeId GetTypeId() {
8425 // The compiler is required to allocate a different
8426 // TypeIdHelper<T>::dummy_ variable for each T used to instantiate
8427 // the template. Therefore, the address of dummy_ is guaranteed to
8428 // be unique.
8429 return &(TypeIdHelper<T>::dummy_);
8430}

8527
8528// State of the definition of a type-parameterized test case.
8529class GTEST_API_ TypedTestCasePState {
8530 public:
8531 TypedTestCasePState() : registered_(false) {}
8532
8533 // Adds the given test name to defined_test_names_ and return true
8534 // if the test case hasn't been registered; otherwise aborts the
8535 // program.
8536 bool AddTestName(const char* file, int line, const char* case_name,
8537 const char* test_name) {
8538 if (registered_) {
8539 fprintf(stderr, "%s Test %s must be defined before "
8540 "REGISTER_TYPED_TEST_CASE_P(%s, ...).\n",
8541 FormatFileLocation(file, line).c_str(), test_name, case_name);
8542 fflush(stderr);
8543 posix::Abort();
8544 }
8545 registered_tests_.insert(
8546 ::std::make_pair(test_name, CodeLocation(file, line)));
8547 return true;
8548 }
8549
8550 bool TestExists(const std::string& test_name) const {
8551 return registered_tests_.count(test_name) > 0;
8552 }
8553
8554 const CodeLocation& GetCodeLocation(const std::string& test_name) const {
8555 RegisteredTestsMap::const_iterator it = registered_tests_.find(test_name);
8556 GTEST_CHECK_(it != registered_tests_.end());
8557 return it->second;
8558 }
8559
8560 // Verifies that registered_tests match the test names in
8561 // defined_test_names_; returns registered_tests if successful, or
8562 // aborts the program otherwise.
8563 const char* VerifyRegisteredTestNames(
8564 const char* file, int line, const char* registered_tests);
8565
8566 private:
8567 typedef ::std::map<std::string, CodeLocation> RegisteredTestsMap;
8568
8569 bool registered_;
8570 RegisteredTestsMap registered_tests_;
8571};

8575// Skips to the first non-space char after the first comma in 'str';
8576// returns NULL if no comma is found in 'str'.
8577inline const char* SkipComma(const char* str) {
8578 const char* comma = strchr(str, ',');
8579 if (comma == NULL) {
8580 return NULL;
8581 }
8582 while (IsSpace(*(++comma))) {}
8583 return comma;
8584}
8585
8586// Returns the prefix of 'str' before the first comma in it; returns
8587// the entire string if it contains no comma.
8588inline std::string GetPrefixUntilComma(const char* str) {
8589 const char* comma = strchr(str, ',');
8590 return comma == NULL ? str : std::string(str, comma);
8591}

8612template <typename NameGenerator>
8613void GenerateNamesRecursively(Types0, std::vector<std::string>*, int) {}
8614
8615template <typename NameGenerator, typename Types>
8616void GenerateNamesRecursively(Types, std::vector<std::string>* result, int i) {
8617 result->push_back(NameGenerator::template GetName<typename Types::Head>(i));
8618 GenerateNamesRecursively<NameGenerator>(typename Types::Tail(), result,
8619 i + 1);
8620}
8621
8622template <typename NameGenerator, typename Types>
8623std::vector<std::string> GenerateNames() {
8624 std::vector<std::string> result;
8625 GenerateNamesRecursively<NameGenerator>(Types(), &result, 0);
8626 return result;
8627}

8629// TypeParameterizedTest<Fixture, TestSel, Types>::Register()
8630// registers a list of type-parameterized tests with Google Test. The
8631// return value is insignificant - we just need to return something
8632// such that we can call this function in a namespace scope.
8633//
8634// Implementation note: The GTEST_TEMPLATE_ macro declares a template
8635// template parameter. It's defined in gtest-type-util.h.
8636template <GTEST_TEMPLATE_ Fixture, class TestSel, typename Types>
8637class TypeParameterizedTest {
8638 public:
8639 // 'index' is the index of the test in the type list 'Types'
8640 // specified in INSTANTIATE_TYPED_TEST_CASE_P(Prefix, TestCase,
8641 // Types). Valid values for 'index' are [0, N - 1] where N is the
8642 // length of Types.
8643 static bool Register(const char* prefix, const CodeLocation& code_location,
8644 const char* case_name, const char* test_names, int index,
8645 const std::vector<std::string>& type_names =
8646 GenerateNames<DefaultNameGenerator, Types>()) {
8647 typedef typename Types::Head Type;
8648 typedef Fixture<Type> FixtureClass;
8649 typedef typename GTEST_BIND_(TestSel, Type) TestClass;
8650
8651 // First, registers the first type-parameterized test in the type
8652 // list.
8653 MakeAndRegisterTestInfo(
8654 (std::string(prefix) + (prefix[0] == '\0' ? "" : "/") + case_name +
8655 "/" + type_names[index])
8656 .c_str(),
8657 StripTrailingSpaces(GetPrefixUntilComma(test_names)).c_str(),
8658 GetTypeName<Type>().c_str(),
8659 NULL, // No value parameter.
8660 code_location, GetTypeId<FixtureClass>(), TestClass::SetUpTestCase,
8661 TestClass::TearDownTestCase, new TestFactoryImpl<TestClass>);
8662
8663 // Next, recurses (at compile time) with the tail of the type list.
8664 return TypeParameterizedTest<Fixture, TestSel,
8665 typename Types::Tail>::Register(prefix,
8666 code_location,
8667 case_name,
8668 test_names,
8669 index + 1,
8670 type_names);
8671 }
8672};
8673
8674// The base case for the compile time recursion.
8675template <GTEST_TEMPLATE_ Fixture, class TestSel>
8676class TypeParameterizedTest<Fixture, TestSel, Types0> {
8677 public:
8678 static bool Register(const char* /*prefix*/, const CodeLocation&,
8679 const char* /*case_name*/, const char* /*test_names*/,
8680 int /*index*/,
8681 const std::vector<std::string>& =
8682 std::vector<std::string>() /*type_names*/) {
8683 return true;
8684 }
8685};
8686
8687// TypeParameterizedTestCase<Fixture, Tests, Types>::Register()
8688// registers *all combinations* of 'Tests' and 'Types' with Google
8689// Test. The return value is insignificant - we just need to return
8690// something such that we can call this function in a namespace scope.
8691template <GTEST_TEMPLATE_ Fixture, typename Tests, typename Types>
8692class TypeParameterizedTestCase {
8693 public:
8694 static bool Register(const char* prefix, CodeLocation code_location,
8695 const TypedTestCasePState* state, const char* case_name,
8696 const char* test_names,
8697 const std::vector<std::string>& type_names =
8698 GenerateNames<DefaultNameGenerator, Types>()) {
8699 std::string test_name = StripTrailingSpaces(
8700 GetPrefixUntilComma(test_names));
8701 if (!state->TestExists(test_name)) {
8702 fprintf(stderr, "Failed to get code location for test %s.%s at %s.",
8703 case_name, test_name.c_str(),
8704 FormatFileLocation(code_location.file.c_str(),
8705 code_location.line).c_str());
8706 fflush(stderr);
8707 posix::Abort();
8708 }
8709 const CodeLocation& test_location = state->GetCodeLocation(test_name);
8710
8711 typedef typename Tests::Head Head;
8712
8713 // First, register the first test in 'Test' for each type in 'Types'.
8714 TypeParameterizedTest<Fixture, Head, Types>::Register(
8715 prefix, test_location, case_name, test_names, 0, type_names);
8716
8717 // Next, recurses (at compile time) with the tail of the test list.
8718 return TypeParameterizedTestCase<Fixture, typename Tests::Tail,
8719 Types>::Register(prefix, code_location,
8720 state, case_name,
8721 SkipComma(test_names),
8722 type_names);
8723 }
8724};
8725
8726// The base case for the compile time recursion.
8727template <GTEST_TEMPLATE_ Fixture, typename Types>
8728class TypeParameterizedTestCase<Fixture, Templates0, Types> {
8729 public:
8730 static bool Register(const char* /*prefix*/, const CodeLocation&,
8731 const TypedTestCasePState* /*state*/,
8732 const char* /*case_name*/, const char* /*test_names*/,
8733 const std::vector<std::string>& =
8734 std::vector<std::string>() /*type_names*/) {
8735 return true;
8736 }
8737};

8791 GTEST_DISALLOW_COPY_AND_ASSIGN_(Random);

8814 typename ::testing::internal::RemoveReference<T>::type

8816// Removes const from a type if it is a const type, otherwise leaves

8824// MSVC 8.0, Sun C++, and IBM XL C++ have a bug which causes the above
8825// definition to fail to remove the const in 'const int[3]' and 'const
8826// char[3][4]'. The following specialization works around the bug.
8827template <typename T, size_t N>
8828struct RemoveConst<const T[N]> {

8830};

8832#if defined(_MSC_VER) && _MSC_VER < 1400

8835// and thus needs to be conditionally compiled.

8837struct RemoveConst<T[N]> {

8851// ImplicitlyConvertible<From, To>::value is a compile-time bool
8852// constant that's true iff type From can be implicitly converted to
8853// type To.
8854template <typename From, typename To>
8855class ImplicitlyConvertible {
8856 private:
8857 // We need the following helper functions only for their types.
8858 // They have no implementations.
8859
8860 // MakeFrom() is an expression whose type is From. We cannot simply
8861 // use From(), as the type From may not have a public default
8862 // constructor.
8863 static typename AddReference<From>::type MakeFrom();
8864
8865 // These two functions are overloaded. Given an expression
8866 // Helper(x), the compiler will pick the first version if x can be
8867 // implicitly converted to type To; otherwise it will pick the
8868 // second version.
8869 //
8870 // The first version returns a value of size 1, and the second
8871 // version returns a value of size 2. Therefore, by checking the
8872 // size of Helper(x), which can be done at compile time, we can tell
8873 // which version of Helper() is used, and hence whether x can be
8874 // implicitly converted to type To.
8875 static char Helper(To);
8876 static char (&Helper(...))[2]; // NOLINT
8877
8878 // We have to put the 'public' section after the 'private' section,
8879 // or MSVC refuses to compile the code.
8880 public:
8881#if defined(__BORLANDC__)
8882 // C++Builder cannot use member overload resolution during template
8883 // instantiation. The simplest workaround is to use its C++0x type traits
8884 // functions (C++Builder 2009 and above only).
8885 static const bool value = __is_convertible(From, To);
8886#else
8887 // MSVC warns about implicitly converting from double to int for
8888 // possible loss of data, so we need to temporarily disable the
8889 // warning.
8890 GTEST_DISABLE_MSC_WARNINGS_PUSH_(4244)
8891 static const bool value =
8892 sizeof(Helper(ImplicitlyConvertible::MakeFrom())) == 1;
8893 GTEST_DISABLE_MSC_WARNINGS_POP_()
8894#endif // __BORLANDC__
8895};
8896template <typename From, typename To>
8897const bool ImplicitlyConvertible<From, To>::value;

8899// IsAProtocolMessage<T>::value is a compile-time bool constant that's
8900// true iff T is type ProtocolMessage, proto2::Message, or a subclass
8901// of those.
8902template <typename T>
8903struct IsAProtocolMessage
8904 : public bool_constant<
8905 ImplicitlyConvertible<const T*, const ::ProtocolMessage*>::value ||
8906 ImplicitlyConvertible<const T*, const ::proto2::Message*>::value> {
8907};

8909// When the compiler sees expression IsContainerTest<C>(0), if C is an
8910// STL-style container class, the first overload of IsContainerTest
8911// will be viable (since both C::iterator* and C::const_iterator* are
8912// valid types and NULL can be implicitly converted to them). It will
8913// be picked over the second overload as 'int' is a perfect match for
8914// the type of argument 0. If C::iterator or C::const_iterator is not
8915// a valid type, the first overload is not viable, and the second
8916// overload will be picked. Therefore, we can determine whether C is
8917// a container class by checking the type of IsContainerTest<C>(0).
8918// The value of the expression is insignificant.
8919//
8920// In C++11 mode we check the existence of a const_iterator and that an
8921// iterator is properly implemented for the container.
8922//
8923// For pre-C++11 that we look for both C::iterator and C::const_iterator.
8924// The reason is that C++ injects the name of a class as a member of the
8925// class itself (e.g. you can refer to class iterator as either
8926// 'iterator' or 'iterator::iterator'). If we look for C::iterator
8927// only, for example, we would mistakenly think that a class named
8928// iterator is an STL container.
8929//
8930// Also note that the simpler approach of overloading
8931// IsContainerTest(typename C::const_iterator*) and
8932// IsContainerTest(...) doesn't work with Visual Age C++ and Sun C++.
8933typedef int IsContainer;
8934#if GTEST_LANG_CXX11
8935template <class C,
8936 class Iterator = decltype(::std::declval<const C&>().begin()),
8937 class = decltype(::std::declval<const C&>().end()),
8938 class = decltype(++::std::declval<Iterator&>()),
8939 class = decltype(*::std::declval<Iterator>()),
8940 class = typename C::const_iterator>
8941IsContainer IsContainerTest(int /* dummy */) {
8942 return 0;
8943}
8944#else
8945template <class C>
8946IsContainer IsContainerTest(int /* dummy */,
8947 typename C::iterator* /* it */ = NULL,
8948 typename C::const_iterator* /* const_it */ = NULL) {
8949 return 0;
8950}
8951#endif // GTEST_LANG_CXX11
8952
8953typedef char IsNotContainer;
8954template <class C>
8955IsNotContainer IsContainerTest(long /* dummy */) { return '\0'; }
8956
8957// Trait to detect whether a type T is a hash table.
8958// The heuristic used is that the type contains an inner type `hasher` and does
8959// not contain an inner type `reverse_iterator`.
8960// If the container is iterable in reverse, then order might actually matter.
8961template <typename T>
8962struct IsHashTable {
8963 private:
8964 template <typename U>
8965 static char test(typename U::hasher*, typename U::reverse_iterator*);
8966 template <typename U>
8967 static int test(typename U::hasher*, ...);
8968 template <typename U>
8969 static char test(...);
8970
8971 public:
8972 static const bool value = sizeof(test<T>(0, 0)) == sizeof(int);
8973};
8974
8975template <typename T>
8976const bool IsHashTable<T>::value;
8977
8978template<typename T>
8979struct VoidT {
8980 typedef void value_type;
8981};
8982
8983template <typename T, typename = void>
8984struct HasValueType : false_type {};
8985template <typename T>
8986struct HasValueType<T, VoidT<typename T::value_type> > : true_type {
8987};
8988
8989template <typename C,
8990 bool = sizeof(IsContainerTest<C>(0)) == sizeof(IsContainer),
8991 bool = HasValueType<C>::value>
8992struct IsRecursiveContainerImpl;
8993
8994template <typename C, bool HV>
8995struct IsRecursiveContainerImpl<C, false, HV> : public false_type {};
8996
8997// Since the IsRecursiveContainerImpl depends on the IsContainerTest we need to
8998// obey the same inconsistencies as the IsContainerTest, namely check if
8999// something is a container is relying on only const_iterator in C++11 and
9000// is relying on both const_iterator and iterator otherwise
9001template <typename C>
9002struct IsRecursiveContainerImpl<C, true, false> : public false_type {};
9003
9004template <typename C>
9005struct IsRecursiveContainerImpl<C, true, true> {
9006 #if GTEST_LANG_CXX11
9007 typedef typename IteratorTraits<typename C::const_iterator>::value_type
9008 value_type;
9009#else
9010 typedef typename IteratorTraits<typename C::iterator>::value_type value_type;
9011#endif
9012 typedef is_same<value_type, C> type;
9013};

9015// IsRecursiveContainer<Type> is a unary compile-time predicate that
9016// evaluates whether C is a recursive container type. A recursive container
9017// type is a container type whose value_type is equal to the container type
9018// itself. An example for a recursive container type is
9019// boost::filesystem::path, whose iterator has a value_type that is equal to
9020// boost::filesystem::path.
9021template <typename C>
9022struct IsRecursiveContainer : public IsRecursiveContainerImpl<C>::type {};

9024// EnableIf<condition>::type is void when 'Cond' is true, and
9025// undefined when 'Cond' is false. To use SFINAE to make a function
9026// overload only apply when a particular expression is true, add
9027// "typename EnableIf<expression>::type* = 0" as the last parameter.
9028template<bool> struct EnableIf;
9029template<> struct EnableIf<true> { typedef void type; }; // NOLINT

9031// Utilities for native arrays.
9032
9033// ArrayEq() compares two k-dimensional native arrays using the
9034// elements' operator==, where k can be any integer >= 0. When k is
9035// 0, ArrayEq() degenerates into comparing a single pair of values.
9036
9037template <typename T, typename U>
9038bool ArrayEq(const T* lhs, size_t size, const U* rhs);
9039
9040// This generic version is used when k is 0.
9041template <typename T, typename U>
9042inline bool ArrayEq(const T& lhs, const U& rhs) { return lhs == rhs; }
9043
9044// This overload is used when k >= 1.
9045template <typename T, typename U, size_t N>
9046inline bool ArrayEq(const T(&lhs)[N], const U(&rhs)[N]) {
9047 return internal::ArrayEq(lhs, N, rhs);
9048}
9049
9050// This helper reduces code bloat. If we instead put its logic inside
9051// the previous ArrayEq() function, arrays with different sizes would
9052// lead to different copies of the template code.
9053template <typename T, typename U>
9054bool ArrayEq(const T* lhs, size_t size, const U* rhs) {
9055 for (size_t i = 0; i != size; i++) {
9056 if (!internal::ArrayEq(lhs[i], rhs[i]))
9057 return false;
9058 }
9059 return true;
9060}
9061
9062// Finds the first element in the iterator range [begin, end) that
9063// equals elem. Element may be a native array type itself.
9064template <typename Iter, typename Element>
9065Iter ArrayAwareFind(Iter begin, Iter end, const Element& elem) {
9066 for (Iter it = begin; it != end; ++it) {
9067 if (internal::ArrayEq(*it, elem))
9068 return it;
9069 }
9070 return end;
9071}
9072
9073// CopyArray() copies a k-dimensional native array using the elements'
9074// operator=, where k can be any integer >= 0. When k is 0,
9075// CopyArray() degenerates into copying a single value.
9076
9077template <typename T, typename U>
9078void CopyArray(const T* from, size_t size, U* to);
9079
9080// This generic version is used when k is 0.
9081template <typename T, typename U>
9082inline void CopyArray(const T& from, U* to) { *to = from; }
9083
9084// This overload is used when k >= 1.
9085template <typename T, typename U, size_t N>
9086inline void CopyArray(const T(&from)[N], U(*to)[N]) {
9087 internal::CopyArray(from, N, *to);
9088}
9089
9090// This helper reduces code bloat. If we instead put its logic inside
9091// the previous CopyArray() function, arrays with different sizes
9092// would lead to different copies of the template code.
9093template <typename T, typename U>
9094void CopyArray(const T* from, size_t size, U* to) {
9095 for (size_t i = 0; i != size; i++) {
9096 internal::CopyArray(from[i], to + i);
9097 }
9098}
9099
9100// The relation between an NativeArray object (see below) and the
9101// native array it represents.
9102// We use 2 different structs to allow non-copyable types to be used, as long
9103// as RelationToSourceReference() is passed.
9104struct RelationToSourceReference {};
9105struct RelationToSourceCopy {};
9106
9107// Adapts a native array to a read-only STL-style container. Instead
9108// of the complete STL container concept, this adaptor only implements
9109// members useful for Google Mock's container matchers. New members
9110// should be added as needed. To simplify the implementation, we only
9111// support Element being a raw type (i.e. having no top-level const or
9112// reference modifier). It's the client's responsibility to satisfy
9113// this requirement. Element can be an array type itself (hence
9114// multi-dimensional arrays are supported).
9115template <typename Element>
9116class NativeArray {
9117 public:
9118 // STL-style container typedefs.
9119 typedef Element value_type;
9120 typedef Element* iterator;
9121 typedef const Element* const_iterator;
9122
9123 // Constructs from a native array. References the source.
9124 NativeArray(const Element* array, size_t count, RelationToSourceReference) {
9125 InitRef(array, count);
9126 }
9127
9128 // Constructs from a native array. Copies the source.
9129 NativeArray(const Element* array, size_t count, RelationToSourceCopy) {
9130 InitCopy(array, count);
9131 }
9132
9133 // Copy constructor.
9134 NativeArray(const NativeArray& rhs) {
9135 (this->*rhs.clone_)(rhs.array_, rhs.size_);
9136 }
9137
9138 ~NativeArray() {
9139 if (clone_ != &NativeArray::InitRef)
9140 delete[] array_;
9141 }
9142
9143 // STL-style container methods.
9144 size_t size() const { return size_; }
9145 const_iterator begin() const { return array_; }
9146 const_iterator end() const { return array_ + size_; }
9147 bool operator==(const NativeArray& rhs) const {
9148 return size() == rhs.size() &&
9149 ArrayEq(begin(), size(), rhs.begin());
9150 }
9151
9152 private:
9153 enum {
9154 kCheckTypeIsNotConstOrAReference = StaticAssertTypeEqHelper<
9155 Element, GTEST_REMOVE_REFERENCE_AND_CONST_(Element)>::value
9156 };
9157
9158 // Initializes this object with a copy of the input.
9159 void InitCopy(const Element* array, size_t a_size) {
9160 Element* const copy = new Element[a_size];
9161 CopyArray(array, a_size, copy);
9162 array_ = copy;
9163 size_ = a_size;
9164 clone_ = &NativeArray::InitCopy;
9165 }
9166
9167 // Initializes this object with a reference of the input.
9168 void InitRef(const Element* array, size_t a_size) {
9169 array_ = array;
9170 size_ = a_size;
9171 clone_ = &NativeArray::InitRef;
9172 }
9173
9174 const Element* array_;
9175 size_t size_;
9176 void (NativeArray::*clone_)(const Element*, size_t);
9177
9178 GTEST_DISALLOW_ASSIGN_(NativeArray);
9179};

9184#define GTEST_MESSAGE_AT_(file, line, message, result_type) \
9185 ::testing::internal::AssertHelper(result_type, file, line, message) \
9186 = ::testing::Message()
9187
9188#define GTEST_MESSAGE_(message, result_type) \
9189 GTEST_MESSAGE_AT_(__FILE__, __LINE__, message, result_type)
9190
9191#define GTEST_FATAL_FAILURE_(message) \
9192 return GTEST_MESSAGE_(message, ::testing::TestPartResult::kFatalFailure)
9193
9194#define GTEST_NONFATAL_FAILURE_(message) \
9195 GTEST_MESSAGE_(message, ::testing::TestPartResult::kNonFatalFailure)
9196
9197#define GTEST_SUCCESS_(message) \
9198 GTEST_MESSAGE_(message, ::testing::TestPartResult::kSuccess)

9200// Suppress MSVC warning 4702 (unreachable code) for the code following
9201// statement if it returns or throws (or doesn't return or throw in some
9202// situations).
9203#define GTEST_SUPPRESS_UNREACHABLE_CODE_WARNING_BELOW_(statement) \
9204 if (::testing::internal::AlwaysTrue()) { statement; }
9205
9206#define GTEST_TEST_THROW_(statement, expected_exception, fail) \
9207 GTEST_AMBIGUOUS_ELSE_BLOCKER_ \
9208 if (::testing::internal::ConstCharPtr gtest_msg = "") { \
9209 bool gtest_caught_expected = false; \
9210 try { \
9211 GTEST_SUPPRESS_UNREACHABLE_CODE_WARNING_BELOW_(statement); \
9212 } \
9213 catch (expected_exception const&) { \
9214 gtest_caught_expected = true; \
9215 } \
9216 catch (...) { \
9217 gtest_msg.value = \
9218 "Expected: " #statement " throws an exception of type " \
9219 #expected_exception ".\n Actual: it throws a different type."; \
9220 goto GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(gtest_label_testthrow_, __LINE__); \
9221 } \
9222 if (!gtest_caught_expected) { \
9223 gtest_msg.value = \
9224 "Expected: " #statement " throws an exception of type " \
9225 #expected_exception ".\n Actual: it throws nothing."; \
9226 goto GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(gtest_label_testthrow_, __LINE__); \
9227 } \
9228 } else \
9229 GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(gtest_label_testthrow_, __LINE__): \
9230 fail(gtest_msg.value)
9231
9232#define GTEST_TEST_NO_THROW_(statement, fail) \
9233 GTEST_AMBIGUOUS_ELSE_BLOCKER_ \
9234 if (::testing::internal::AlwaysTrue()) { \
9235 try { \
9236 GTEST_SUPPRESS_UNREACHABLE_CODE_WARNING_BELOW_(statement); \
9237 } \
9238 catch (const std::exception& e) { \
9239 std::cerr << "Exception message: " << e.what() << std::endl; \
9240 goto GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(gtest_label_testnothrow_, __LINE__); \
9241 } \
9242 catch (...) { \
9243 goto GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(gtest_label_testnothrow_, __LINE__); \
9244 } \
9245 } else \
9246 GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(gtest_label_testnothrow_, __LINE__): \
9247 fail("Expected: " #statement " doesn't throw an exception.\n" \
9248 " Actual: it throws.")
9249
9250#define GTEST_TEST_ANY_THROW_(statement, fail) \
9251 GTEST_AMBIGUOUS_ELSE_BLOCKER_ \
9252 if (::testing::internal::AlwaysTrue()) { \
9253 bool gtest_caught_any = false; \
9254 try { \
9255 GTEST_SUPPRESS_UNREACHABLE_CODE_WARNING_BELOW_(statement); \
9256 } \
9257 catch (...) { \
9258 gtest_caught_any = true; \
9259 } \
9260 if (!gtest_caught_any) { \
9261 goto GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(gtest_label_testanythrow_, __LINE__); \
9262 } \
9263 } else \
9264 GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(gtest_label_testanythrow_, __LINE__): \
9265 fail("Expected: " #statement " throws an exception.\n" \
9266 " Actual: it doesn't.")
9267
9268
9269// Implements Boolean test assertions such as EXPECT_TRUE. expression can be
9270// either a boolean expression or an AssertionResult. text is a textual
9271// representation of expression as it was passed into the EXPECT_TRUE.
9272#define GTEST_TEST_BOOLEAN_(expression, text, actual, expected, fail) \
9273 GTEST_AMBIGUOUS_ELSE_BLOCKER_ \
9274 if (const ::testing::AssertionResult gtest_ar_ = \
9275 ::testing::AssertionResult(expression)) \
9276 ; \
9277 else \
9278 fail(::testing::internal::GetBoolAssertionFailureMessage(\
9279 gtest_ar_, text, #actual, #expected).c_str())
9280
9281#define GTEST_TEST_NO_FATAL_FAILURE_(statement, fail) \
9282 GTEST_AMBIGUOUS_ELSE_BLOCKER_ \
9283 if (::testing::internal::AlwaysTrue()) { \
9284 ::testing::internal::HasNewFatalFailureHelper gtest_fatal_failure_checker; \
9285 GTEST_SUPPRESS_UNREACHABLE_CODE_WARNING_BELOW_(statement); \
9286 if (gtest_fatal_failure_checker.has_new_fatal_failure()) { \
9287 goto GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(gtest_label_testnofatal_, __LINE__); \
9288 } \
9289 } else \
9290 GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(gtest_label_testnofatal_, __LINE__): \
9291 fail("Expected: " #statement " doesn't generate new fatal " \
9292 "failures in the current thread.\n" \
9293 " Actual: it does.")
9294
9295// Expands to the name of the class that implements the given test.
9296#define GTEST_TEST_CLASS_NAME_(test_case_name, test_name) \
9297 test_case_name##_##test_name##_Test
9298
9299// Helper macro for defining tests.
9300#define GTEST_TEST_(test_case_name, test_name, parent_class, parent_id)\
9301class GTEST_TEST_CLASS_NAME_(test_case_name, test_name) : public parent_class {\
9302 public:\
9303 GTEST_TEST_CLASS_NAME_(test_case_name, test_name)() {}\
9304 private:\
9305 virtual void TestBody();\
9306 static ::testing::TestInfo* const test_info_ GTEST_ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED_;\
9307 GTEST_DISALLOW_COPY_AND_ASSIGN_(\
9308 GTEST_TEST_CLASS_NAME_(test_case_name, test_name));\
9309};\
9310\
9311::testing::TestInfo* const GTEST_TEST_CLASS_NAME_(test_case_name, test_name)\
9312 ::test_info_ =\
9313 ::testing::internal::MakeAndRegisterTestInfo(\
9314 #test_case_name, #test_name, NULL, NULL, \
9315 ::testing::internal::CodeLocation(__FILE__, __LINE__), \
9316 (parent_id), \
9317 parent_class::SetUpTestCase, \
9318 parent_class::TearDownTestCase, \
9319 new ::testing::internal::TestFactoryImpl<\
9320 GTEST_TEST_CLASS_NAME_(test_case_name, test_name)>);\
9321void GTEST_TEST_CLASS_NAME_(test_case_name, test_name)::TestBody()

9420// DeathTest is a class that hides much of the complexity of the
9421// GTEST_DEATH_TEST_ macro. It is abstract; its static Create method
9422// returns a concrete class that depends on the prevailing death test
9423// style, as defined by the --gtest_death_test_style and/or
9424// --gtest_internal_run_death_test flags.
9425
9426// In describing the results of death tests, these terms are used with
9427// the corresponding definitions:
9428//
9429// exit status: The integer exit information in the format specified
9430// by wait(2)
9431// exit code: The integer code passed to exit(3), _exit(2), or
9432// returned from main()
9433class GTEST_API_ DeathTest {
9434 public:
9435 // Create returns false if there was an error determining the
9436 // appropriate action to take for the current death test; for example,
9437 // if the gtest_death_test_style flag is set to an invalid value.
9438 // The LastMessage method will return a more detailed message in that
9439 // case. Otherwise, the DeathTest pointer pointed to by the "test"
9440 // argument is set. If the death test should be skipped, the pointer
9441 // is set to NULL; otherwise, it is set to the address of a new concrete
9442 // DeathTest object that controls the execution of the current test.
9443 static bool Create(const char* statement, const RE* regex,
9444 const char* file, int line, DeathTest** test);
9445 DeathTest();
9446 virtual ~DeathTest() { }
9447
9448 // A helper class that aborts a death test when it's deleted.
9449 class ReturnSentinel {
9450 public:
9451 explicit ReturnSentinel(DeathTest* test) : test_(test) { }
9452 ~ReturnSentinel() { test_->Abort(TEST_ENCOUNTERED_RETURN_STATEMENT); }
9453 private:
9454 DeathTest* const test_;
9455 GTEST_DISALLOW_COPY_AND_ASSIGN_(ReturnSentinel);
9456 } GTEST_ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED_;
9457
9458 // An enumeration of possible roles that may be taken when a death
9459 // test is encountered. EXECUTE means that the death test logic should
9460 // be executed immediately. OVERSEE means that the program should prepare
9461 // the appropriate environment for a child process to execute the death
9462 // test, then wait for it to complete.
9463 enum TestRole { OVERSEE_TEST, EXECUTE_TEST };
9464
9465 // An enumeration of the three reasons that a test might be aborted.
9466 enum AbortReason {
9467 TEST_ENCOUNTERED_RETURN_STATEMENT,
9468 TEST_THREW_EXCEPTION,
9469 TEST_DID_NOT_DIE
9470 };
9471
9472 // Assumes one of the above roles.
9473 virtual TestRole AssumeRole() = 0;

9476 virtual int Wait() = 0;

9480 // predicate, and its stderr output matches a user-supplied regular
9481 // expression.

9483 // than a function pointer or functor, or else Wait and Passed could
9484 // be combined.

9487 // Signals that the death test did not die as expected.
9488 virtual void Abort(AbortReason reason) = 0;

9490 // Returns a human-readable outcome message regarding the outcome of
9491 // the last death test.
9492 static const char* LastMessage();
9493
9494 static void set_last_death_test_message(const std::string& message);
9495
9496 private:
9497 // A string containing a description of the outcome of the last death test.
9498 static std::string last_death_test_message_;

9524// Traps C++ exceptions escaping statement and reports them as test
9525// failures. Note that trapping SEH exceptions is not implemented here.
9526# if GTEST_HAS_EXCEPTIONS
9527# define GTEST_EXECUTE_DEATH_TEST_STATEMENT_(statement, death_test) \
9528 try { \
9529 GTEST_SUPPRESS_UNREACHABLE_CODE_WARNING_BELOW_(statement); \
9530 } catch (const ::std::exception& gtest_exception) { \
9531 fprintf(\
9532 stderr, \
9533 "\n%s: Caught std::exception-derived exception escaping the " \
9534 "death test statement. Exception message: %s\n", \
9535 ::testing::internal::FormatFileLocation(__FILE__, __LINE__).c_str(), \
9536 gtest_exception.what()); \
9537 fflush(stderr); \
9538 death_test->Abort(::testing::internal::DeathTest::TEST_THREW_EXCEPTION); \
9539 } catch (...) { \
9540 death_test->Abort(::testing::internal::DeathTest::TEST_THREW_EXCEPTION); \
9541 }
9542
9543# else
9544# define GTEST_EXECUTE_DEATH_TEST_STATEMENT_(statement, death_test) \
9545 GTEST_SUPPRESS_UNREACHABLE_CODE_WARNING_BELOW_(statement)
9546
9547# endif
9548
9549// This macro is for implementing ASSERT_DEATH*, EXPECT_DEATH*,
9550// ASSERT_EXIT*, and EXPECT_EXIT*.
9551# define GTEST_DEATH_TEST_(statement, predicate, regex, fail) \
9552 GTEST_AMBIGUOUS_ELSE_BLOCKER_ \
9553 if (::testing::internal::AlwaysTrue()) { \
9554 const ::testing::internal::RE& gtest_regex = (regex); \
9555 ::testing::internal::DeathTest* gtest_dt; \
9556 if (!::testing::internal::DeathTest::Create(#statement, &gtest_regex, \
9557 __FILE__, __LINE__, &gtest_dt)) { \
9558 goto GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(gtest_label_, __LINE__); \
9559 } \
9560 if (gtest_dt != NULL) { \
9561 ::testing::internal::scoped_ptr< ::testing::internal::DeathTest> \
9562 gtest_dt_ptr(gtest_dt); \
9563 switch (gtest_dt->AssumeRole()) { \
9564 case ::testing::internal::DeathTest::OVERSEE_TEST: \
9565 if (!gtest_dt->Passed(predicate(gtest_dt->Wait()))) { \
9566 goto GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(gtest_label_, __LINE__); \
9567 } \
9568 break; \
9569 case ::testing::internal::DeathTest::EXECUTE_TEST: { \
9570 ::testing::internal::DeathTest::ReturnSentinel \
9571 gtest_sentinel(gtest_dt); \
9572 GTEST_EXECUTE_DEATH_TEST_STATEMENT_(statement, gtest_dt); \
9573 gtest_dt->Abort(::testing::internal::DeathTest::TEST_DID_NOT_DIE); \
9574 break; \
9575 } \
9576 default: \
9577 break; \
9578 } \
9579 } \
9580 } else \
9581 GTEST_CONCAT_TOKEN_(gtest_label_, __LINE__): \
9582 fail(::testing::internal::DeathTest::LastMessage())
9583// The symbol "fail" here expands to something into which a message
9584// can be streamed.
9585
9586// This macro is for implementing ASSERT/EXPECT_DEBUG_DEATH when compiled in
9587// NDEBUG mode. In this case we need the statements to be executed and the macro
9588// must accept a streamed message even though the message is never printed.
9589// The regex object is not evaluated, but it is used to prevent "unused"
9590// warnings and to avoid an expression that doesn't compile in debug mode.
9591#define GTEST_EXECUTE_STATEMENT_(statement, regex) \
9592 GTEST_AMBIGUOUS_ELSE_BLOCKER_ \
9593 if (::testing::internal::AlwaysTrue()) { \
9594 GTEST_SUPPRESS_UNREACHABLE_CODE_WARNING_BELOW_(statement); \
9595 } else if (!::testing::internal::AlwaysTrue()) { \
9596 const ::testing::internal::RE& gtest_regex = (regex); \
9597 static_cast<void>(gtest_regex); \
9598 } else \
9599 ::testing::Message()

9666// The following macros are useful for writing death tests.
9667
9668// Here's what happens when an ASSERT_DEATH* or EXPECT_DEATH* is
9669// executed:
9670//
9671// 1. It generates a warning if there is more than one active
9672// thread. This is because it's safe to fork() or clone() only
9673// when there is a single thread.
9674//
9675// 2. The parent process clone()s a sub-process and runs the death
9676// test in it; the sub-process exits with code 0 at the end of the
9677// death test, if it hasn't exited already.
9678//
9679// 3. The parent process waits for the sub-process to terminate.
9680//
9681// 4. The parent process checks the exit code and error message of
9682// the sub-process.
9683//
9684// Examples:
9685//
9686// ASSERT_DEATH(server.SendMessage(56, "Hello"), "Invalid port number");
9687// for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
9688// EXPECT_DEATH(server.ProcessRequest(i),
9689// "Invalid request .* in ProcessRequest()")
9690// << "Failed to die on request " << i;
9691// }
9692//
9693// ASSERT_EXIT(server.ExitNow(), ::testing::ExitedWithCode(0), "Exiting");
9694//
9695// bool KilledBySIGHUP(int exit_code) {
9696// return WIFSIGNALED(exit_code) && WTERMSIG(exit_code) == SIGHUP;
9697// }
9698//
9699// ASSERT_EXIT(client.HangUpServer(), KilledBySIGHUP, "Hanging up!");
9700//
9701// On the regular expressions used in death tests:
9702//
9703// GOOGLETEST_CM0005 DO NOT DELETE
9704// On POSIX-compliant systems (*nix), we use the <regex.h> library,
9705// which uses the POSIX extended regex syntax.
9706//
9707// On other platforms (e.g. Windows or Mac), we only support a simple regex
9708// syntax implemented as part of Google Test. This limited
9709// implementation should be enough most of the time when writing
9710// death tests; though it lacks many features you can find in PCRE
9711// or POSIX extended regex syntax. For example, we don't support
9712// union ("x|y"), grouping ("(xy)"), brackets ("[xy]"), and
9713// repetition count ("x{5,7}"), among others.
9714//
9715// Below is the syntax that we do support. We chose it to be a
9716// subset of both PCRE and POSIX extended regex, so it's easy to
9717// learn wherever you come from. In the following: 'A' denotes a
9718// literal character, period (.), or a single \\ escape sequence;
9719// 'x' and 'y' denote regular expressions; 'm' and 'n' are for
9720// natural numbers.
9721//
9722// c matches any literal character c
9723// \\d matches any decimal digit
9724// \\D matches any character that's not a decimal digit
9725// \\f matches \f
9726// \\n matches \n
9727// \\r matches \r
9728// \\s matches any ASCII whitespace, including \n
9729// \\S matches any character that's not a whitespace
9730// \\t matches \t
9731// \\v matches \v
9732// \\w matches any letter, _, or decimal digit
9733// \\W matches any character that \\w doesn't match
9734// \\c matches any literal character c, which must be a punctuation
9735// . matches any single character except \n
9736// A? matches 0 or 1 occurrences of A
9737// A* matches 0 or many occurrences of A
9738// A+ matches 1 or many occurrences of A
9739// ^ matches the beginning of a string (not that of each line)
9740// $ matches the end of a string (not that of each line)
9741// xy matches x followed by y
9742//
9743// If you accidentally use PCRE or POSIX extended regex features
9744// not implemented by us, you will get a run-time failure. In that
9745// case, please try to rewrite your regular expression within the
9746// above syntax.
9747//
9748// This implementation is *not* meant to be as highly tuned or robust
9749// as a compiled regex library, but should perform well enough for a
9750// death test, which already incurs significant overhead by launching
9751// a child process.
9752//
9753// Known caveats:
9754//
9755// A "threadsafe" style death test obtains the path to the test
9756// program from argv[0] and re-executes it in the sub-process. For
9757// simplicity, the current implementation doesn't search the PATH
9758// when launching the sub-process. This means that the user must
9759// invoke the test program via a path that contains at least one
9760// path separator (e.g. path/to/foo_test and
9761// /absolute/path/to/bar_test are fine, but foo_test is not). This
9762// is rarely a problem as people usually don't put the test binary
9763// directory in PATH.
9764//
9765// FIXME: make thread-safe death tests search the PATH.
9766
9767// Asserts that a given statement causes the program to exit, with an
9768// integer exit status that satisfies predicate, and emitting error output
9769// that matches regex.
9770# define ASSERT_EXIT(statement, predicate, regex) \
9771 GTEST_DEATH_TEST_(statement, predicate, regex, GTEST_FATAL_FAILURE_)
9772
9773// Like ASSERT_EXIT, but continues on to successive tests in the
9774// test case, if any:
9775# define EXPECT_EXIT(statement, predicate, regex) \
9776 GTEST_DEATH_TEST_(statement, predicate, regex, GTEST_NONFATAL_FAILURE_)
9777
9778// Asserts that a given statement causes the program to exit, either by
9779// explicitly exiting with a nonzero exit code or being killed by a
9780// signal, and emitting error output that matches regex.
9781# define ASSERT_DEATH(statement, regex) \
9782 ASSERT_EXIT(statement, ::testing::internal::ExitedUnsuccessfully, regex)
9783
9784// Like ASSERT_DEATH, but continues on to successive tests in the
9785// test case, if any:
9786# define EXPECT_DEATH(statement, regex) \
9787 EXPECT_EXIT(statement, ::testing::internal::ExitedUnsuccessfully, regex)

9816// EXPECT_DEBUG_DEATH asserts that the given statements die in debug mode.
9817// The death testing framework causes this to have interesting semantics,
9818// since the sideeffects of the call are only visible in opt mode, and not
9819// in debug mode.
9820//
9821// In practice, this can be used to test functions that utilize the
9822// LOG(DFATAL) macro using the following style:
9823//
9824// int DieInDebugOr12(int* sideeffect) {
9825// if (sideeffect) {
9826// *sideeffect = 12;
9827// }
9828// LOG(DFATAL) << "death";
9829// return 12;
9830// }
9831//
9832// TEST(TestCase, TestDieOr12WorksInDgbAndOpt) {
9833// int sideeffect = 0;
9834// // Only asserts in dbg.
9835// EXPECT_DEBUG_DEATH(DieInDebugOr12(&sideeffect), "death");
9836//
9837// #ifdef NDEBUG
9838// // opt-mode has sideeffect visible.
9839// EXPECT_EQ(12, sideeffect);
9840// #else
9841// // dbg-mode no visible sideeffect.
9842// EXPECT_EQ(0, sideeffect);
9843// #endif
9844// }
9845//
9846// This will assert that DieInDebugReturn12InOpt() crashes in debug
9847// mode, usually due to a DCHECK or LOG(DFATAL), but returns the
9848// appropriate fallback value (12 in this case) in opt mode. If you
9849// need to test that a function has appropriate side-effects in opt
9850// mode, include assertions against the side-effects. A general
9851// pattern for this is:
9852//
9853// EXPECT_DEBUG_DEATH({
9854// // Side-effects here will have an effect after this statement in
9855// // opt mode, but none in debug mode.
9856// EXPECT_EQ(12, DieInDebugOr12(&sideeffect));
9857// }, "death");
9858//
9859# ifdef NDEBUG
9860
9861# define EXPECT_DEBUG_DEATH(statement, regex) \
9862 GTEST_EXECUTE_STATEMENT_(statement, regex)
9863
9864# define ASSERT_DEBUG_DEATH(statement, regex) \
9865 GTEST_EXECUTE_STATEMENT_(statement, regex)
9866
9867# else
9868
9869# define EXPECT_DEBUG_DEATH(statement, regex) \
9870 EXPECT_DEATH(statement, regex)
9871
9872# define ASSERT_DEBUG_DEATH(statement, regex) \
9873 ASSERT_DEATH(statement, regex)
9874
9875# endif // NDEBUG for EXPECT_DEBUG_DEATH
9876#endif // GTEST_HAS_DEATH_TEST

9878// This macro is used for implementing macros such as
9879// EXPECT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED and ASSERT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED on systems where
9880// death tests are not supported. Those macros must compile on such systems
9881// iff EXPECT_DEATH and ASSERT_DEATH compile with the same parameters on
9882// systems that support death tests. This allows one to write such a macro
9883// on a system that does not support death tests and be sure that it will
9884// compile on a death-test supporting system. It is exposed publicly so that
9885// systems that have death-tests with stricter requirements than
9886// GTEST_HAS_DEATH_TEST can write their own equivalent of
9887// EXPECT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED and ASSERT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED.
9888//
9889// Parameters:
9890// statement - A statement that a macro such as EXPECT_DEATH would test
9891// for program termination. This macro has to make sure this
9892// statement is compiled but not executed, to ensure that
9893// EXPECT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED compiles with a certain
9894// parameter iff EXPECT_DEATH compiles with it.
9895// regex - A regex that a macro such as EXPECT_DEATH would use to test
9896// the output of statement. This parameter has to be
9897// compiled but not evaluated by this macro, to ensure that
9898// this macro only accepts expressions that a macro such as
9899// EXPECT_DEATH would accept.
9900// terminator - Must be an empty statement for EXPECT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED
9901// and a return statement for ASSERT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED.
9902// This ensures that ASSERT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED will not
9903// compile inside functions where ASSERT_DEATH doesn't
9904// compile.
9905//
9906// The branch that has an always false condition is used to ensure that
9907// statement and regex are compiled (and thus syntactically correct) but
9908// never executed. The unreachable code macro protects the terminator
9909// statement from generating an 'unreachable code' warning in case
9910// statement unconditionally returns or throws. The Message constructor at
9911// the end allows the syntax of streaming additional messages into the
9912// macro, for compilational compatibility with EXPECT_DEATH/ASSERT_DEATH.
9913# define GTEST_UNSUPPORTED_DEATH_TEST(statement, regex, terminator) \
9914 GTEST_AMBIGUOUS_ELSE_BLOCKER_ \
9915 if (::testing::internal::AlwaysTrue()) { \
9916 GTEST_LOG_(WARNING) \
9917 << "Death tests are not supported on this platform.\n" \
9918 << "Statement '" #statement "' cannot be verified."; \
9919 } else if (::testing::internal::AlwaysFalse()) { \
9920 ::testing::internal::RE::PartialMatch(".*", (regex)); \
9921 GTEST_SUPPRESS_UNREACHABLE_CODE_WARNING_BELOW_(statement); \
9922 terminator; \
9923 } else \
9924 ::testing::Message()

9926// EXPECT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED(statement, regex) and
9927// ASSERT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED(statement, regex) expand to real death tests if
9928// death tests are supported; otherwise they just issue a warning. This is
9929// useful when you are combining death test assertions with normal test
9930// assertions in one test.
9931#if GTEST_HAS_DEATH_TEST
9932# define EXPECT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED(statement, regex) \
9933 EXPECT_DEATH(statement, regex)
9934# define ASSERT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED(statement, regex) \
9935 ASSERT_DEATH(statement, regex)
9936#else
9937# define EXPECT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED(statement, regex) \
9938 GTEST_UNSUPPORTED_DEATH_TEST(statement, regex, )
9939# define ASSERT_DEATH_IF_SUPPORTED(statement, regex) \
9940 GTEST_UNSUPPORTED_DEATH_TEST(statement, regex, return)

10058// * InstantiationName/FooTest.DoesBlah/0 for "meeny"
10059// * InstantiationName/FooTest.DoesBlah/1 for "miny"
10060// * InstantiationName/FooTest.DoesBlah/2 for "moe"
10061// * InstantiationName/FooTest.HasBlahBlah/0 for "meeny"
10062// * InstantiationName/FooTest.HasBlahBlah/1 for "miny"
10063// * InstantiationName/FooTest.HasBlahBlah/2 for "moe"
10064//
10065// You can use these names in --gtest_filter.
10066//
10067// This statement will instantiate all tests from FooTest again, each
10068// with parameter values "cat" and "dog":
10069
10070const char* pets[] = {"cat", "dog"};
10071INSTANTIATE_TEST_CASE_P(AnotherInstantiationName, FooTest, ValuesIn(pets));
10072
10073// The tests from the instantiation above will have these names:
10074//
10075// * AnotherInstantiationName/FooTest.DoesBlah/0 for "cat"
10076// * AnotherInstantiationName/FooTest.DoesBlah/1 for "dog"
10077// * AnotherInstantiationName/FooTest.HasBlahBlah/0 for "cat"
10078// * AnotherInstantiationName/FooTest.HasBlahBlah/1 for "dog"
10079//
10080// Please note that INSTANTIATE_TEST_CASE_P will instantiate all tests
10081// in the given test case, whether their definitions come before or
10082// AFTER the INSTANTIATE_TEST_CASE_P statement.
10083//
10084// Please also note that generator expressions (including parameters to the
10085// generators) are evaluated in InitGoogleTest(), after main() has started.
10086// This allows the user on one hand, to adjust generator parameters in order
10087// to dynamically determine a set of tests to run and on the other hand,
10088// give the user a chance to inspect the generated tests with Google Test
10089// reflection API before RUN_ALL_TESTS() is executed.
10090//
10091// You can see samples/sample7_unittest.cc and samples/sample8_unittest.cc
10092// for more examples.
10093//
10094// In the future, we plan to publish the API for defining new parameter
10095// generators. But for now this interface remains part of the internal
10096// implementation and is subject to change.
10097//
10098//
10099// A parameterized test fixture must be derived from testing::Test and from
10100// testing::WithParamInterface<T>, where T is the type of the parameter
10101// values. Inheriting from TestWithParam<T> satisfies that requirement because
10102// TestWithParam<T> inherits from both Test and WithParamInterface. In more
10103// complicated hierarchies, however, it is occasionally useful to inherit
10104// separately from Test and WithParamInterface. For example:
10105
10106class BaseTest : public ::testing::Test {
10107 // You can inherit all the usual members for a non-parameterized test
10108 // fixture here.
10109};
10110
10111class DerivedTest : public BaseTest, public ::testing::WithParamInterface<int> {
10112 // The usual test fixture members go here too.
10113};
10114
10115TEST_F(BaseTest, HasFoo) {
10116 // This is an ordinary non-parameterized test.
10117}
10118
10119TEST_P(DerivedTest, DoesBlah) {
10120 // GetParam works just the same here as if you inherit from TestWithParam.
10121 EXPECT_TRUE(foo.Blah(GetParam()));
10122}
10123

10203//
10204// A "smart" pointer type with reference tracking. Every pointer to a
10205// particular object is kept on a circular linked list. When the last pointer
10206// to an object is destroyed or reassigned, the object is deleted.
10207//
10208// Used properly, this deletes the object when the last reference goes away.
10209// There are several caveats:
10210// - Like all reference counting schemes, cycles lead to leaks.
10211// - Each smart pointer is actually two pointers (8 bytes instead of 4).
10212// - Every time a pointer is assigned, the entire list of pointers to that
10213// object is traversed. This class is therefore NOT SUITABLE when there
10214// will often be more than two or three pointers to a particular object.
10215// - References are only tracked as long as linked_ptr<> objects are copied.
10216// If a linked_ptr<> is converted to a raw pointer and back, BAD THINGS
10217// will happen (double deletion).
10218//
10219// A good use of this class is storing object references in STL containers.
10220// You can safely put linked_ptr<> in a vector<>.
10221// Other uses may not be as good.
10222//
10223// Note: If you use an incomplete type with linked_ptr<>, the class
10224// *containing* linked_ptr<> must have a constructor and destructor (even
10225// if they do nothing!).
10226//
10227// Bill Gibbons suggested we use something like this.
10228//
10229// Thread Safety:
10230// Unlike other linked_ptr implementations, in this implementation
10231// a linked_ptr object is thread-safe in the sense that:
10232// - it's safe to copy linked_ptr objects concurrently,
10233// - it's safe to copy *from* a linked_ptr and read its underlying
10234// raw pointer (e.g. via get()) concurrently, and
10235// - it's safe to write to two linked_ptrs that point to the same
10236// shared object concurrently.
10237// FIXME: rename this to safe_linked_ptr to avoid
10238// confusion with normal linked_ptr.
10239
10240// GOOGLETEST_CM0001 DO NOT DELETE
10241
10242#ifndef GTEST_INCLUDE_GTEST_INTERNAL_GTEST_LINKED_PTR_H_
10243#define GTEST_INCLUDE_GTEST_INTERNAL_GTEST_LINKED_PTR_H_
10244
10245#include <stdlib.h>
10246#include <assert.h>

10249namespace testing {
10250namespace internal {
10251
10252// Protects copying of all linked_ptr objects.
10253GTEST_API_ GTEST_DECLARE_STATIC_MUTEX_(g_linked_ptr_mutex);
10254
10255// This is used internally by all instances of linked_ptr<>. It needs to be
10256// a non-template class because different types of linked_ptr<> can refer to
10257// the same object (linked_ptr<Superclass>(obj) vs linked_ptr<Subclass>(obj)).
10258// So, it needs to be possible for different types of linked_ptr to participate
10259// in the same circular linked list, so we need a single class type here.
10260//
10261// DO NOT USE THIS CLASS DIRECTLY YOURSELF. Use linked_ptr<T>.
10262class linked_ptr_internal {
10263 public:
10264 // Create a new circle that includes only this instance.
10265 void join_new() {
10266 next_ = this;
10267 }
10268
10269 // Many linked_ptr operations may change p.link_ for some linked_ptr
10270 // variable p in the same circle as this object. Therefore we need
10271 // to prevent two such operations from occurring concurrently.
10272 //
10273 // Note that different types of linked_ptr objects can coexist in a
10274 // circle (e.g. linked_ptr<Base>, linked_ptr<Derived1>, and
10275 // linked_ptr<Derived2>). Therefore we must use a single mutex to
10276 // protect all linked_ptr objects. This can create serious
10277 // contention in production code, but is acceptable in a testing
10278 // framework.
10279
10280 // Join an existing circle.
10281 void join(linked_ptr_internal const* ptr)
10282 GTEST_LOCK_EXCLUDED_(g_linked_ptr_mutex) {
10283 MutexLock lock(&g_linked_ptr_mutex);
10284
10285 linked_ptr_internal const* p = ptr;
10286 while (p->next_ != ptr) {
10287 assert(p->next_ != this &&
10288 "Trying to join() a linked ring we are already in. "
10289 "Is GMock thread safety enabled?");
10290 p = p->next_;
10291 }
10292 p->next_ = this;
10293 next_ = ptr;
10294 }
10295
10296 // Leave whatever circle we're part of. Returns true if we were the
10297 // last member of the circle. Once this is done, you can join() another.
10298 bool depart()
10299 GTEST_LOCK_EXCLUDED_(g_linked_ptr_mutex) {
10300 MutexLock lock(&g_linked_ptr_mutex);
10301
10302 if (next_ == this) return true;
10303 linked_ptr_internal const* p = next_;
10304 while (p->next_ != this) {
10305 assert(p->next_ != next_ &&
10306 "Trying to depart() a linked ring we are not in. "
10307 "Is GMock thread safety enabled?");
10308 p = p->next_;
10309 }
10310 p->next_ = next_;
10311 return false;
10312 }
10313
10314 private:
10315 mutable linked_ptr_internal const* next_;
10316};
10317
10318template <typename T>
10319class linked_ptr {
10320 public:
10321 typedef T element_type;
10322
10323 // Take over ownership of a raw pointer. This should happen as soon as
10324 // possible after the object is created.
10325 explicit linked_ptr(T* ptr = NULL) { capture(ptr); }
10326 ~linked_ptr() { depart(); }
10327
10328 // Copy an existing linked_ptr<>, adding ourselves to the list of references.
10329 template <typename U> linked_ptr(linked_ptr<U> const& ptr) { copy(&ptr); }
10330 linked_ptr(linked_ptr const& ptr) { // NOLINT
10331 assert(&ptr != this);
10332 copy(&ptr);
10333 }
10334
10335 // Assignment releases the old value and acquires the new.
10336 template <typename U> linked_ptr& operator=(linked_ptr<U> const& ptr) {
10337 depart();
10338 copy(&ptr);
10339 return *this;
10340 }
10341
10342 linked_ptr& operator=(linked_ptr const& ptr) {
10343 if (&ptr != this) {
10344 depart();
10345 copy(&ptr);
10346 }
10347 return *this;
10348 }
10349
10350 // Smart pointer members.
10351 void reset(T* ptr = NULL) {
10352 depart();
10353 capture(ptr);
10354 }
10355 T* get() const { return value_; }
10356 T* operator->() const { return value_; }
10357 T& operator*() const { return *value_; }
10358
10359 bool operator==(T* p) const { return value_ == p; }
10360 bool operator!=(T* p) const { return value_ != p; }
10361 template <typename U>
10362 bool operator==(linked_ptr<U> const& ptr) const {
10363 return value_ == ptr.get();
10364 }
10365 template <typename U>
10366 bool operator!=(linked_ptr<U> const& ptr) const {
10367 return value_ != ptr.get();
10368 }
10369
10370 private:
10371 template <typename U>
10372 friend class linked_ptr;
10373
10374 T* value_;
10375 linked_ptr_internal link_;
10376
10377 void depart() {
10378 if (link_.depart()) delete value_;
10379 }
10380
10381 void capture(T* ptr) {
10382 value_ = ptr;
10383 link_.join_new();
10384 }
10385
10386 template <typename U> void copy(linked_ptr<U> const* ptr) {
10387 value_ = ptr->get();
10388 if (value_)
10389 link_.join(&ptr->link_);
10390 else
10391 link_.join_new();
10392 }
10393};
10394
10395template<typename T> inline
10396bool operator==(T* ptr, const linked_ptr<T>& x) {
10397 return ptr == x.get();
10398}
10399
10400template<typename T> inline
10401bool operator!=(T* ptr, const linked_ptr<T>& x) {
10402 return ptr != x.get();
10403}
10404
10405// A function to convert T* into linked_ptr<T>
10406// Doing e.g. make_linked_ptr(new FooBarBaz<type>(arg)) is a shorter notation
10407// for linked_ptr<FooBarBaz<type> >(new FooBarBaz<type>(arg))
10408template <typename T>
10409linked_ptr<T> make_linked_ptr(T* ptr) {
10410 return linked_ptr<T>(ptr);
10411}

10447// Google Test - The Google C++ Testing and Mocking Framework
10448//
10449// This file implements a universal value printer that can print a
10450// value of any type T:
10451//
10452// void ::testing::internal::UniversalPrinter<T>::Print(value, ostream_ptr);
10453//
10454// A user can teach this function how to print a class type T by
10455// defining either operator<<() or PrintTo() in the namespace that
10456// defines T. More specifically, the FIRST defined function in the
10457// following list will be used (assuming T is defined in namespace
10458// foo):
10459//
10460// 1. foo::PrintTo(const T&, ostream*)
10461// 2. operator<<(ostream&, const T&) defined in either foo or the
10462// global namespace.
10463//
10464// However if T is an STL-style container then it is printed element-wise
10465// unless foo::PrintTo(const T&, ostream*) is defined. Note that
10466// operator<<() is ignored for container types.
10467//
10468// If none of the above is defined, it will print the debug string of
10469// the value if it is a protocol buffer, or print the raw bytes in the
10470// value otherwise.
10471//
10472// To aid debugging: when T is a reference type, the address of the
10473// value is also printed; when T is a (const) char pointer, both the
10474// pointer value and the NUL-terminated string it points to are
10475// printed.
10476//
10477// We also provide some convenient wrappers:
10478//
10479// // Prints a value to a string. For a (const or not) char
10480// // pointer, the NUL-terminated string (but not the pointer) is
10481// // printed.
10482// std::string ::testing::PrintToString(const T& value);
10483//
10484// // Prints a value tersely: for a reference type, the referenced
10485// // value (but not the address) is printed; for a (const or not) char
10486// // pointer, the NUL-terminated string (but not the pointer) is
10487// // printed.
10488// void ::testing::internal::UniversalTersePrint(const T& value, ostream*);
10489//
10490// // Prints value using the type inferred by the compiler. The difference
10491// // from UniversalTersePrint() is that this function prints both the
10492// // pointer and the NUL-terminated string for a (const or not) char pointer.
10493// void ::testing::internal::UniversalPrint(const T& value, ostream*);
10494//
10495// // Prints the fields of a tuple tersely to a string vector, one
10496// // element for each field. Tuple support must be enabled in
10497// // gtest-port.h.
10498// std::vector<string> UniversalTersePrintTupleFieldsToStrings(
10499// const Tuple& value);
10500//
10501// Known limitation:
10502//
10503// The print primitives print the elements of an STL-style container
10504// using the compiler-inferred type of *iter where iter is a
10505// const_iterator of the container. When const_iterator is an input
10506// iterator but not a forward iterator, this inferred type may not
10507// match value_type, and the print output may be incorrect. In
10508// practice, this is rarely a problem as for most containers
10509// const_iterator is a forward iterator. We'll fix this if there's an
10510// actual need for it. Note that this fix cannot rely on value_type
10511// being defined as many user-defined container types don't have
10512// value_type.
10513
10514// GOOGLETEST_CM0001 DO NOT DELETE
10515
